notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on 2 Samuel 23, drawn from the approved sites.

---

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into two distinct parts: verses 1–7, "the last words of David" — his final inspired poetic utterance; and verses 8–39, a roll-call of David's mighty warriors. The psalm was not included in the Book of Psalms because it is not a hymn for public worship but a personal, prophetic testament. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

---

## Part 1: David's Last Words (vv. 1–7)

### v. 1 — "These are the last words of David…"

**What "last words" means.** These are not literally the final words David ever spoke (he later gave instructions to Solomon about the temple), but his last recorded poetic and prophetic composition, or his last words spoken under divine inspiration. Gill says they were "the last after he had finished the book of Psalms; or the last that he spoke under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit." Clarke suggests "the last poetical composition" is intended — he may have spoken many words after in prose but none in verse. — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**The four self-descriptions.** The writer (not David himself — this is the narrator's introduction, per Bible.org) gives four titles that encapsulate David's life:

- *"The son of Jesse"* — his humble origin as a farmer's son (Enduring Word).
- *"The man raised up on high"* — from sheepfold to throne; God did the raising, not self-promotion (Gill, Enduring Word).
- *"The anointed of the God of Jacob"* — divinely chosen and empowered; Gill notes this ties to Samuel's anointing and connects David to the covenant God of Israel.
- *"The sweet psalmist of Israel"* — literally "pleasant in the songs of Israel." Gill says David "composed most of the psalms and hymns of praise," invented tunes, and appointed singers. — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm ; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**The word "oracle" / "said."** The Hebrew word *ne'um* is a term for a divine utterance. Ellicott notes it is used "between two and three hundred times" of direct divine utterances, and applied to human sayings only here, in Numbers 24 (Balaam), and Proverbs 30:1 (Agur) — each a special claim to inspiration. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**Typology.** Gill sees David here as a type of Christ: "a branch out of the root of Jesse, highly exalted … anointed to be prophet, priest, and King; and who sweetly expounded the psalms concerning himself." — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm

---

### v. 2 — "The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue."

**Explicit claim to divine inspiration.** David knew — at least at times — that he was speaking under the Spirit's guidance. Ellicott calls this "most explicit assertion that this was spoken under the prompting and guidance of the Divine Spirit." Gill says the psalms "were not the fruits of his own genius, but were written by him under the inspiration of the Spirit of God," and notes that the Spirit spoke "in me" — first internally impressed on his mind, then expressed with his tongue. He also says "the very words in which they are delivered were given to him" — a verbal-plenary view of inspiration. — Ellicott & Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**New Testament connection.** 2 Peter 1:21 and Acts 1:16 are cited to support David as a prophet moved by the Holy Spirit. — Bible.org: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/21-profiles-courage-2-samuel-23

---

### v. 3 — "The God of Israel spoke; the Rock of Israel said to me, 'He who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God…'"

**"The Rock of Israel."** A title for God (cf. 2 Sam 22:3), emphasising His perfect reliability in what He declares. Ellicott notes it is appropriate here "to show the perfect reliability of what God declares." Gill expands to see a Trinitarian hint: "the God of Israel, Jehovah the Father; the Rock of Israel, Jehovah the Son; and the Spirit of Jehovah, as in 2 Samuel 23:2, who is Jehovah the Spirit." — Ellicott & Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**The just ruler.** "The fundamental point of all just government has never been more perfectly set forth — that it must be 'in the fear of God'" (Ellicott). Enduring Word says this is the key to justice: rulers who fear God recognise that a God of justice will review their work. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**Messianic interpretation.** The Targum (ancient Aramaic paraphrase) applies these words directly to the Messiah: "The true Judge said, he would appoint to me a King, who is the Messiah, who shall arise and rule in the fear of the Lord." Gill says the character applies in all respects to the Messiah, who is just and upon whom "the Spirit of the fear of the Lord rests" (Isaiah 11:1–2). — Gill & Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm

---

### v. 4 — "is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn, the glistening after the rain on the sprouting grass of the earth."

**The imagery of blessed rule.** The just ruler's reign is compared to two natural phenomena:

1. **A cloudless morning sunrise** — light, clarity, joy, and ever-increasing brightness. Gill elaborates: "his administrations are pleasant and delightful, and promise a growing and increasing happiness to them, like the morning light and rising sun." Applied to Christ, "the sun of righteousness then arose, and scattered the darkness of the night."

2. **Sunshine after rain making grass spring up** — life-giving, productive, refreshing. The combination of rain and sun produces flourishing growth; so the righteous king produces a flourishing people.

— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**The verse as a connecting hinge.** Ellicott suggests the grammar flows directly into v. 5: "as by means of sunlight and by means of rain the tender grass grows from the earth — is not my house so with God?" This reading connects the ideal of vv. 3–4 with David's confession or question in v. 5. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**Christological reading.** Bible.org notes that Jesus seems to have drawn on the imagery of this passage: comparing Himself to "light" (John 8:12; 9:5) and in the parable of the weeds being burned (Matthew 13:30, 40). — Bible.org: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/21-profiles-courage-2-samuel-23

---

### v. 5 — "Is not my house right with God? For He has established with me an everlasting covenant…"

**The major translation divide.** This verse is among the most debated in the chapter. Two opposite readings exist:

- **Negative/confessional reading** (KJV, NKJV): *"Although my house is not so with God, yet He has made with me an everlasting covenant…"* — David humbly admits his house falls short of the ideal, but trusts God's covenant anyway. This is the reading of the LXX, Vulgate, and Syriac (the ancient versions). Ellicott says this "gives a higher idea of David's spiritual discernment."

- **Positive/interrogative reading** (NASB, NIV, ESV, BSB): *"Is not my house right with God? For He has made with me an everlasting covenant…"* — David confidently declares that God has indeed made his house right through the covenant. Most modern commentators prefer this.

Bible.org concludes: "Either way, the sense of David's words is clear. In the first instance, David would be stressing his unworthiness … in contrast with God's grace … In the second instance, David would still be emphasizing God's grace to him."

— Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm ; Bible.org: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/21-profiles-courage-2-samuel-23 ; Enduring Word (which takes the negative reading): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**"Everlasting covenant."** This refers to the Davidic Covenant of 2 Samuel 7:12–16 — God's promise that David's throne would endure forever. It reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ. The Berean Study Bible notes that the covenant is "ordered and secured" — "its divine origin and unchangeable nature," meticulously planned by God. — https://biblehub.com/study/2_samuel/23.htm

**"Ordered in all things, and sure."** Ellicott: "As a carefully drawn legal document, providing for all contingencies and leaving no room for misconstruction." Gill: "It is ordered in all things: to promote and advance the glory of all the three Persons in the Godhead … to secure the persons of the saints, and to provide everything needful for them for time and eternity." — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm

**"All my salvation and all my desire."** Enduring Word: David only said this because the covenant was based on God's faithfulness, not his own. "David knew that his own obedience was not enough to be a foundation for all his salvation and all his desire." Some take "all my desire" to refer to Christ Himself — Gill supplies it: "he is … to whom is all their desire; and in whom is all their delight." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/ ; Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm

---

### v. 6 — "But the worthless are all like thorns raked aside…"

**"Worthless" = sons of Belial.** The Hebrew uses a strong abstract form meaning "worthlessness." These are those who cast off God's authority. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**The imagery.** Unlike the tender grass (v. 4) that flourishes under the king's reign, the wicked are thorns — useless, harmful, not gathered or stored. They cannot be picked up by hand without injury. Enduring Word explains: David knew that God would oppose "the sons of rebellion" and they would end in ruin. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**Bible.org** notes the contrast with v. 4: "When the righteous King of Israel (Jesus Christ) comes to rule … His kingdom causes the righteous to flourish … But the wicked are not likened to grass; they are compared to thorns." — Bible.org: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/21-profiles-courage-2-samuel-23

---

### v. 7 — "The man who touches them must be armed with iron … The fire burns them to ashes in the place where they lie."

**Handling thorns requires tools.** Thorns must be handled with an iron hook or spear-shaft — they cannot be managed bare-handed. Ellicott describes it as "an iron hook on the end of a spear staff." — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**Final judgment by fire.** The thorns are "utterly burned with fire in their place." This is an image of final, in-place destruction. Gill applies it historically to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Roman armies, and eschatologically to final judgment when the wicked are "cast into the lake which burns with fire and brimstone." The Targum also applies it to the great day of judgment. — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/23.htm

**"In the place where they lie" / "in the same place."** The phrase is used only here, and its meaning is uncertain. Vulgate: "to nothing" (utter destruction); LXX: "shame." The English rendering is "as well sustained as any" (Ellicott). — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**The Targum's Messianic summary.** The ancient Jewish Targum on vv. 1–3 is a greatly expanded paraphrase applying the whole oracle to the Messiah and the end of the age. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

---

## Part 2: David's Mighty Men (vv. 8–39)

### v. 8 — "Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite was chief of the Three…"

The list begins with the "first three" — the most elite warriors. The name in Chronicles (1 Chron 11:11) is Jashobeam the Hachmonite. Ellicott says the text of this verse "has undergone several alterations, which may be corrected by the parallel passage." He wielded his spear against 800 men (Chronicles says 300 — Gill suggests two separate battles, or a copyist's error). — Ellicott & Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm ; GotQuestions: https://www.gotquestions.org/mighty-men-David.html

Joab is conspicuously absent from the list — as commander-in-chief, he stood in a rank by himself (Ellicott).

---

### vv. 9–10 — Eleazar son of Dodo

Eleazar fought alongside David when the men of Israel retreated. He "stood his ground and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword." Ellicott notes: "Instances are rare, but well authenticated, of a sort of cramp following excessive exertion, so that the hand could only be released from the sword by external appliances." The victory is credited to the LORD. Ellicott clarifies that "the people returned after him only to plunder" does not imply they deserted him but that "they turned wherever he went to gather the spoil." — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**Spurgeon (via Enduring Word)** saw Eleazar as a model for solitary Christian witness: "Solitary prowess is expected of believers … Dare to be an Eleazar, and go forth and smite the Philistines alone." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

---

### vv. 11–12 — Shammah son of Agee

When the Philistines banded together at a field full of lentils and Israel's troops fled, Shammah "took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines." The victory is again attributed to the LORD. The field of lentils represents the Philistines' attempt to plunder Israel's food supply. Ellicott notes that Chronicles has "barley" instead of "lentils" — the Hebrew words are easily confused but the point is the same. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

---

### vv. 13–17 — The water from Bethlehem's well

**The setting.** Three of the thirty chief men went to David at the cave of Adullam during harvest, while a Philistine garrison occupied Bethlehem. Ellicott clarifies these are not the same three as vv. 8–12 (no definite article) — they were another elite three, two probably being Abishai and Benaiah. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

**David's longing.** David did not command anyone; he simply voiced a nostalgic wish for water from the well by the gate of Bethlehem, his boyhood home. Enduring Word notes this was "not a command or even a request, just a vocalized longing." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**The exploit.** The three broke through the Philistine camp, drew water, and brought it to David — risking their lives for their king's mere wish. This shows "the personal power of David over his followers and the enthusiasm with which he inspired them" (Ellicott).

**David pours it out.** David refused to drink, instead pouring it out "to the LORD." Ellicott explains: "The word is the technical term for the sacrificial libation, and David assimilated his act to a sacrifice by a solemn consecration of this dangerously won water to the Lord." David calls the water "the blood of the men who risked their lives" — to him it was as sacred as life-blood itself (cf. Lev 17:10–11). — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

Enduring Word: "David was so honored by the self-sacrifice of these three mighty men he felt that the water was too good for him – and worthy to be poured out in sacrifice to the LORD." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

---

### vv. 18–19 — Abishai

Abishai, Joab's brother, was "chief of the Three" (or "chief among three" — a second triad). He killed 300 men with his spear. He was more honoured than the Three yet not included among the original Three (vv. 8–12). Ellicott says "the three" here are the triad of heroes just mentioned in vv. 13–17. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

---

### vv. 20–23 — Benaiah son of Jehoiada

Benaiah was from Kabzeel (a town on the extreme south of Judah, on the border of Edom — Ellicott). His exploits:

- **Struck down two "champions" (or "lion-like men") of Moab.** The Hebrew is literally "lion of God" — an expression for great warriors (Ellicott).
- **Killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day.** A remarkable feat. Gill notes the treacherous conditions.
- **Killed a huge Egyptian** by going against him with only a club, seizing the Egyptian's spear, and killing him with his own weapon.

Ellicott adds that Benaiah later became general of the third army division and, for his loyalty to Solomon during Adonijah's rebellion, was made commander-in-chief (1 Kings 2:25–35). He was over David's guard — the Hebrew word translated "guard" may mean "private audience" or council (Ellicott). — Ellicott & Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm

---

### vv. 24–39 — The Thirty (actually thirty-seven)

**The list.** These men formed the elite corps known as "the Thirty," though the chapter lists thirty-seven names. This may reflect replacements when members died, or the number was approximate — a title rather than a precise count. StudyLight.org (Pett's Commentary) suggests "it was more of a title for the group than a number to be taken literally." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/2-samuel-23.html

**Notable names:**

- **Asahel** (v. 24) — Joab's brother, killed by Abner early in David's reign. His inclusion shows the list is not restricted to one time (Ellicott).
- **Eliam son of Ahithophel** (v. 34) — Possibly the father of Bathsheba (2 Sam 11:3). Ellicott says it is "interesting to know that a son of David's astute but treacherous counsellor was among his thirty heroes." Enduring Word notes: "When David heard of Bathsheba's relation to Uriah and Eliam and Ahithophel … he should have put away every idea of adultery."
- **Uriah the Hittite** (v. 39) — The last name listed. A foreigner (like Zelek the Ammonite and Igal of Zobah) who rose to distinction, probably a proselyte. His inclusion "shows the tragic irony: this faithful warrior whose wife David took was numbered among his most honored followers" (Enduring Word). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**Thirty-seven total.** The count works as: three in the first class (vv. 8–12), two in the second (Abishai and Benaiah, vv. 18–23), and thirty-two in the third (vv. 24–39) — yielding thirty-seven. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/23-39.html

**The transformation theme.** Enduring Word and Bible.org both stress that these men did not start as great warriors — many were the "distressed, indebted, and discontented" who gathered to David at Adullam (1 Sam 22:1–2). David's leadership transformed them. "More than all his victories against outside foes, the influence of his life and character on the men nearest to him testify to his essential greatness" (G. Campbell Morgan, cited by Enduring Word). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

---

## Traditional Readings — Summary of Consensus

Across the sources consulted, there is broad agreement that:

1. **David's last words are a prophetic oracle** claiming direct divine inspiration (the Spirit spoke through him).
2. **The just ruler described in vv. 3–4 is ultimately messianic** — pointing to Jesus Christ, the perfect Davidic king. This is the ancient Jewish Targum's reading, the typical Christian reading, and is reflected even in Jesus' own use of the "light" imagery.
3. **The "everlasting covenant"** is the Davidic Covenant of 2 Samuel 7, fulfilled in Christ.
4. **The wicked as thorns** depicts final judgment — a warning that accompanies the promise of salvation.
5. **David's mighty men** illustrate how God uses loyal followers to build His kingdom, and how divine victory (the LORD brought about a great victory) works through human courage.

---

## Distinctive Traditions

**Baptist (Calvinistic/Spurgeon):** Charles Spurgeon, cited by Enduring Word, emphasizes individual Christian courage: Eleazar standing alone is a type of the believer who "dares to stand alone." Spurgeon also notes these men "came to David when his fortunes were at the lowest ebb … Happy are they who can follow a good cause in its worst estate, for theirs is true glory." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-23/

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** The emphasis on the Spirit's inspiration in v. 2 is highlighted as David's conscious awareness of the Spirit speaking through him — a point that resonates with charismatic emphases on the Holy Spirit's active role. Guzik also stresses the transformation of the mighty men from distressed outcasts to heroes, a theme of personal transformation.

**The KJV/NKJV vs. Modern Translations Divide on v. 5:** The older Protestant translations (KJV, NKJV) preserve the negative/confessional reading ("Although my house be not so with God"), which emphasizes David's humility and unworthiness — a reading that harmonises with Reformed emphases on grace alone. Most modern translations take the positive/interrogative. This is a genuine translation difference, not a doctrinal one — the underlying Hebrew admits both. — Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm ; Bible.org: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/21-profiles-courage-2-samuel-23

**Lutheran:** I was unable to retrieve specific Lutheran commentary from the approved Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) within the fetch/search limits. The traditional Lutheran reading would align with the confessional interpretation of v. 5 and the Christological reading of the just ruler, consistent with the law–gospel hermeneutic.

**Catholic and Orthodox:** I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic commentary from newadvent.org or catholic.com, or Orthodox commentary from oca.org, within the search/fetch limits. The Vulgate's rendering of v. 5 ("Although my house be not so…") aligns with the traditional Catholic reading of David's humility. The Catholic Good News Translation (GNT) takes the positive reading: "And that is how God will bless my descendants…" — https://mail.biblehub.com/catholic/2_samuel/23-5.htm

**Modern Scholarship (textual issues):** The NET Bible notes (referenced indirectly through Bible.org and Ellicott) highlight significant textual variations between 2 Samuel 23 and the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11, including differing name forms and the 800 vs. 300 discrepancy. The variations are generally attributed to scribal transmission over centuries. Ellicott's commentary carefully notes many of these. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/23.htm
